speaker: J. Kenji López-Alt
title: S1E3 Celebrity Chef J. Kenji López-Alt
question: In home cooking, what actually happens when you wash raw chicken before roasting, searing, or grilling it?
guest: For any kind of Western, European, or American-style cooking, I don't wash it. If I'm roasting my chicken, searing some chicken breast, or grilling some chicken, I don't wash it. First of all, the difference between washing and not washing for those types is mainly down to how it's going to come out when you cook, because you don't want to be adding extra water. It takes a lot of energy to evaporate moisture from the surface of meats, and energy you're using to evaporate moisture is being taken away from good browning or good crisping, so you don't want to add moisture to your meat. And the science actually shows that when you wash your chicken in the sink, you're more likely to spread bacteria around your kitchen—let it splash up onto your counter—than you are to actually clean anything that doesn't need cleaning off the chicken anyways. It's worse in almost every way to wash your chicken.

points.core: Evaporating added surface water steals heat needed to brown the chicken.
points.note: Accept: surface moisture absorbing thermal energy, steaming instead of searing/crisping, delayed Maillard browning. Do not credit: vague claims that wet chicken tastes worse without citing evaporative heat loss.

points.core: Rinsing raw chicken in a sink splashes bacteria onto nearby kitchen surfaces.
points.note: Accept: cross-contamination via water droplets or aerosols splashing onto counters, sinks, or utensils. Do not credit: generic food-safety warnings that omit the splashing/spreading mechanism.

points.core: Washing raw poultry fails to remove contaminants that cooking would not eliminate.
points.note: Accept: rinsing does not meaningfully sanitize chicken or clean anything that heat will not kill anyway. Do not credit: both-sides hedging claiming washing is still helpful for cleanliness.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Washing raw chicken doesn't make it safer; it mostly spreads bacteria around your kitchen. Rinsing can't remove pathogens like Salmonella and Campylobacter, which cling tightly to the meat, but the splashing water carries them onto the sink, faucet, countertops, nearby dishes, and foods. In a USDA observational study, about 60% of people who washed poultry had bacteria in their sink afterward, and roughly a quarter contaminated a salad they prepared alongside it. Even without visible splashing, contaminated hands and sink surfaces transfer germs onward.

The step that actually kills the bacteria is cooking: bringing the chicken to an internal temperature of 165°F (74°C) destroys them, whether or not you rinsed first.

Washing also works against good cooking. A wet surface steams before it browns, so you get paler, flabbier skin and a weaker sear. If you want to remove slime or bone fragments, pat the chicken with paper towels instead, then discard them and wash your hands. If you do rinse anyway (for example, after brining), do it gently in a cleared sink, then sanitize the sink and surrounding surfaces.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Washing raw chicken neither cleans the meat nor improves how it cooks; instead, it creates both a food-safety hazard and a culinary disadvantage. Pathogens like *Salmonella* and *Campylobacter* cling tightly to poultry surfaces and crevices and cannot be rinsed off with water—only cooking to an internal temperature of 165°F (74°C) destroys them. Under a running faucet, water droplets rebound off the bird and splash contaminated mist up to three feet across your sink, countertops, utensils, and nearby foods, significantly increasing the risk of cross-contamination.

From a cooking standpoint, rinsing saturates the skin and outer meat with excess water, which directly sabotages roasting, searing, and grilling. Because surface water must boil away at 212°F (100°C) before the Maillard browning reaction can begin around 280°F (140°C), wet chicken steams instead of browning. That added moisture produces pale, rubbery skin in the oven, dangerous hot-oil splatter and gray meat in a skillet, and sticking on grill grates. For safer prep and a crisp, deeply browned crust, skip the sink and blot raw chicken dry with disposable paper towels before seasoning.
